newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil mining giant set to go on the auction block.
newsitem.headline: Brazil mining giant set to go on the auction block.

text.p: Brazil's six-year-old privatisation programme was expected reach its high point this week at the auction of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, the jewel in the Brazilian public sector crown.

With more than two years of planning involved, the auction will kick-off the biggest state selloff in Latin American history and once completed, should raise at least $5 billion for government coffers.
Although a number of legal challenges threaten to delay the sale, planned for Tuesday, government officials were confident they could get around the obstacles and keep to their schedule.

"This is the culmination of two years in which the government has committed itself to the task of transferring to private hands another major provider of goods and services," said Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros, head of the National Development Bank, which is responsible for the privatisation programme.

"Vale" -- as the company is universally known -- stands out among Latin American public sector corporations principally because it is profitable, efficient and innovative in the use of mining technologies.
With more than 15,400 employees, annual revenues of $5 billion and total assets of $10.4 billion, Vale posted a 1996 profit of $632 million.
Its Carajas mine, deep in the Amazon rain forest, holds enough iron ore to secure 400 years of production. Besides aluminum and paper and pulp holdings, Vale mines gold, manganese and bauxite.
If pulled off without snags, the Vale sale should also bury lingering concerns over President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's committment to transform the Brazilian economy.
In more than two years since he was sworn into office, Cardoso has had only moderate success in advancing an ambitious legislative reform agenda.
What is more, the total value of assets privatised under the Cardoso administration falls short of those sold by his predecessor, Itamar Franco.

Analysts say that placing Vale in private hands would send a powerful signal that Brazil's governing elite has finally become convinced that the country's future growth can only be financed through private investment.
Two groups have registered to participate in Tuesday's auction.
One is led by Grupo Votorantim, one of Brazil's largest private conglomerates. It also includes Anglo American Corp. of South Africa Ltd and Japan's Nippon Steel Corp., among others.
The second group is led by Companhia Siderurgica Nacional, a Brazilian steelmaker, and includes Nations Bank, Alcoa, Banco Safra as well as several Brazilian pension funds.

Government planners sighed with relief when the two groups confirmed their interest in Vale. The government needed at least two competing bidders to demonstrate to the world that the auction would be transparent and to show Brazilians that private investors were eager to buy up the company.
For all these reasons the Vale sale has generated bitter opposition from just about every sector of Brazilian society.
Over the past few weeks unions, congressmen, state employees, landless peasants, artists, two former presidents and even Catholic bishops have expressed resistance to the company's privatisation.

"I oppose the sale (because) the government has not explained why it wants to sell and because it hasn't encouraged a debate. Vale turns a profit," said leftist congressman Miro Texeira, a leader of congressional efforts to stop the sale.
The government has still not cleared the legal minefield layed out to stop Tuesday's privatisation auction, but is confident the toughest resistance has already been overcome.
The government was expected on Monday to successfully overturn an injunction granted late Friday that suspended the auction based on alleged irregularities in the proposed bidding process.

Planning Ministry sources said their only real concern was a court case currently in the hands of a Rio de Janeiro judge who has a record of issuing last-minute injunctions which have delayed, but never derailed, previous privatisation auctions.
